title: Form, Function And Buildings That Outlive Their Uses
text:
The phrase 'form follows function' has done more work than almost any other slogan in architecture, and it is worth examining what it actually claimed. Louis Sullivan coined it in the 1890s, arguing that the shape of a building should arise from its purpose as naturally as the shape of an organism arises from its way of life. For a generation of modernists that became a licence to strip away inherited ornament: if a feature served no purpose, it had no business on the building.

The trouble appears when you ask over what period a function is supposed to hold. Buildings outlast their uses. A Georgian terrace designed for a household with servants now holds flats, offices and a dental surgery, and it accommodates them because its rooms are generously sized and largely undifferentiated. A mid-century hospital wing, fitted precisely to the medical practice of its own decade, becomes obsolete when that practice moves on, and it is expensive to adapt. This is why many architects now argue for what they call loose fit: build generously, leave the plan adaptable, and expect the use to change. On a long enough view, the most functional building may be the one that was never designed too tightly around a function.
points: Louis Sullivan coined the phrase in the 1890s, comparing a building's shape to an organism's.
Modernists used it to justify stripping away ornament that served no purpose.
The difficulty is that buildings outlast the uses they were designed for.
A Georgian terrace adapts to new uses because its rooms are large and undifferentiated.
A tightly specified building, such as a mid-century hospital wing, becomes obsolete and costly to adapt.
Architects now favour loose fit: generous, adaptable plans that expect the use to change.
